**1. Plan the day before.**  
If possible, I check my calendar the night before and color in the blocks that are just me and my laptop. If there’s a window that’s still called “meeting,” I note which ones can’t be moved. If you can, swap one of the long chains for something that can be bled into a real break. Sometimes you can ask the right person to end early or start late.

**2. Pack my water and a protein bar before I leave.**  
If I’m not getting a real minute, I need something to chew on. A protein bar and a bottle of water is the only thing that’ll keep me from feeling like I’m just spinning. Same for you—something to crunch on, or at least a sip.

**3. I set the timer in my head.**  
Every 15 minutes, I count. If I’m in a huddle, I’ll say, “three, four, five—stop. real second. breath.” That’s all I get. If I’m lucky, someone else’s phone’s screen is up and I can stare at the blue light for a second and pretend I’m not in here with them.

**4. I write things down on a notepad after each meeting.**  
Not the talking, not the talking. I get the names, the next person, the next time, the one thing that actually matters. If I can’t get it all, I just get the first three things and forget the rest. If I don’t have a notepad, I use my phone. But I write it down, so I don’t have to remember it in my head.

**5. I try to end the last one early.**  
If I know we’re running out of time, I ask for five more minutes to get my notes together. If I can’t, I just keep my mouth shut and pretend I’m listening. That’s the only way you get through it. Sometimes you just have to let the next person start before you’re done.

**6. I text my boss at the end and say I’ll send the notes in ten minutes.**  
If I can, I send the real summary after everyone’s gone. If not, I just hope I didn me something right.

And then I wait until the next one starts and start again. It’s not pretty, but it’s the same every day. You can’t change the schedule, but you can make the mess a little less messy. And if you don’t, you just remember what you said in the third meeting and pray it’s the important one.

Building trust with someone you’ll be working with closely isn’t a one-size-fits-all process, but there are some reliable steps that almost always help. Here’s how I’d approach it—same principles work whether it’s a colleague, vendor, or partner:

1. **Be honest from the start.** If I can’t say something, I say less. If I have to change my mind, I say so and explain why. That’s the only way their “yes” will mean anything.

2. **Follow through on what I say I’ll do.** People notice when promises get made and kept. Small things matter—like returning a file by the deadline or labeling the right boxes. Consistency is the only way to make it real.

3. share the plan, not just the results. If I’m going to reorganize the files, I’ll show you the new system before it goes live. You need to see the map, not just the destination.

4. ask the right questions. If something feels off, I check in. “Is this still the timeline?” or “Should we double-check this calculation?” That’s not micromanaging—it’s making sure we’re both moving forward together.

5. admit when I’m wrong. If I miss a step, I own it and say so. It’s not about being perfect, it’s about making it clear nobody’s hiding in the shadows.

6. give credit where it’s due. If someone else nails a part of the project, I make sure you see it. Trust grows when people can see the pieces fit, not just when the whole thing works.

7. keep the lines open. A quick check-in, even when things look fine, makes it clear we’re still talking. No one can read my mind, but I’ll send the chart so you can see it.

If you do all that, eventually they’ll stop second-guessing. They’ll start trusting the next thing I say. That’s the only way it sticks.

This is a question a lot of us wrestle with—how to actually *be there* for the people who need me, but still carve out space to get things done the right way. It’s not a one-size-fits-all thing, but here’s how I’d think about it, and how you could too.

**1. Block time, not just erase it.**  
Put the meeting or call in my calendar, same as everyone else. Then I check my phone every five minutes before and after, but that’s it. If someone’s waiting, they’ll see I’m busy and they’ll have to wait. If it’s urgent, they’ll know to call the line. It’s about making the time sacred, not just saying I’ll be there at 3pm and then sneaking out at 3:10.

**22. Say “not now, but maybe tomorrow” with a smile.**  
If I can’t do it today, I say it. I don’t make up some other time I can’t keep. People get it. If it can’t wait, then it can’t wait. That’s honesty, not slacking.

**3. I keep a list of my real priorities.**  
Before I say yes to anything, I ask: does this move the big stuff forward? If it doesn’t, I say no, or I reschedule it for a time that fits my work blocks. If it does, I make sure I have the time after it’s done, not before. That’s the only way I’ll finish the project at 2am again.

**4. I let people know when I’m in the zone.**  
If I’m deep in a chunk, I put my status to “do not disturb” and I don’t answer till I’m done. If someone really needs me, they know to wait. If it’s life or death, they can call the phone outside the door. I don the headphones and that’s it.

**5. I negotiate new times, not old ones.**  
If someone’s waiting and I can’t help, I move it to my next window. I don’t fake being free at 4:15 because I was free at 4:10. That’s just cheating me.

**6. I let the day breathe.**  
I don’t check email or DMs every five minutes. I check at the start and the end. If something’s burning, it’ll be in the pile. If it can wait, it waits. If it can’t, it gets pushed to the next day. That’s how I keep the work done, not the mess piling up.

**7. I tell people how it’ll be.**  
I explain the blocks, the windows, the rules. If they can’t work with it, they can find someone who will. That way, we’re both on the same page, not just pretending we are.

It’s not perfect. But it’s honest, and it lets the right things get done, and the right people know when they can count on me and when they’ll have to wait. That’s all I need.

That’s a big, beautiful question—and one that’s been asked in every age. Prophecy and revelation, in the old sense—words spoken by God to people so they’d know what to do before the ground even trembles—seems to have stopped, at least in the way we used to measure it. But maybe that’s just the way we’re looking for it now.

Here’s what I see, and what a lot of people keep asking:

**1. The Silence Isn’t Always There.**  
Sometimes it’s in the numbers, not the voices. The data, the patterns in the weather, the way a city grows, the way a disease spreads—those are signs, if you know how to read them. And sometimes it’s in the dream of a kid in a schoolyard, or the way a scientist sees a cell split in half and writes it down before the rest of the world even notices. So revelation can be in the equations, the blood tests, the satellite images. We just have to look harder.

**2. The Word Gets rewritten.**  
When a doctor finds a cure in the statistics, or a farmer knows the rain won’t come because the clouds are wrong, that’s revelation in a lab coat. The map on my phone? That’s a thousand prophets mapping the world in 1812, folded into a rectangle and sent to everyone for free. We just call it GPS now.

**3. The Voice is Louder in the Question.**  
Maybe the real prophecy is in the questions we can’t answer. The climate’s changing, the languages are melting, the kids on TikTok are laughing at words that shouldn’t exist. We don’t get a sign from above, but the world itself is shaking. That’s a kind of revelation, too—a tremor you can feel in your bones.

**4. The Church is Quiet, but the Fire’s Still There.**  
A lot of people say the last vision was in 1914, or in the smoke, or in the blood at Jaramae. But the hunger for meaning, the way people gather in the dark hoping for a sign, that’s the same. Maybe the fire’s just smaller now, hidden in the light. Or maybe it’s in the hands that build the well so more kids can drink.

**5. We’re all supposed to see it.**  
If God’s still speaking, why would He wait for the next thunderstorm to drop the answer? We’re supposed to look at the cracks in the pavement, the way the river bends, the way someone’s eyes go glassy when they see the truth. That’s the old way or the new way—it doesn’t matter. We’re still supposed to see it.

So I think the prophecy’s in the waiting, in the trembling ground, in the way the numbers add up wrong and the kids in the back of the bus start whispering again. We just have to be awake enough to see it, and brave enough to say it out loud. That’s what I think revelation looks like now. Not in a voice, but in the world itself—waiting for us to look closer.

What about you? Are you looking for a sign, or just trying to see it in the noise?

That’s a big question, and the answer depends on who’s asking and what they’re looking for. But let’s break it down—tradition and progress aren’t enemies, and they don’t have to cancel each other out. Here’s how I see it:

**Tradition is the map. Progress is the new road.**  
People have been following old ways for thousands of years—how we light a fire, how we plant seeds, how we write a letter, how we say hello. Those ways worked for someone, somewhere, once. They carry meaning, memory, and comfort in them. But they weren’t made for every storm or every sun. 

Progress isn’t about tearing up the map. It’s about finding a better path, or a way that lets more people walk through without stepping on each other’s toes. Sometimes the old road still works. Sometimes it’s just a shortcut to the same place. Sometimes it’s a wall.

What happens when you build a new door and forget the old one is still locked? You lose half the story. When you burn the map because you think you’ve found the destination, you might miss the whole forest. 

So, I think the real relationship is this: you need both. You need to know how we got here, why we do things the way we do, and what we lost when we stopped looking. But you also need to keep asking if there’s a better way, and if the old way is just a cage we painted for ourselves. 

Sometimes tradition saves us from forgetting. Sometimes progress saves us from dying. But if we only walk forward or only look back, we’re just lost. 

That’s how I see it.
